figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: From the Mediterranean, natural size, seen from below; central mouth surrounded by a wreath of short lip fringes opens into a flat stomach cavity with 32 radial canals bearing gonads midway along their course and short tentacles at the margin, with an inward horizontal muscle ring (Velum).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: From New Guinea, natural size, side view; the transparent jelly disc forms a crystal-like disc with 32 grooves on its upper surface and 16 long, very mobile tentacles at the margin.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: From New Guinea, natural size, view from below; the circular mouth with 16 curled lobes leads to a stomach cavity with 16 forked radial canals, each fork bearing a sausage-shaped gonad, numerous small statocyst granules on the nerve ring, and an inward horizontal muscle ring (Velum).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: From Helgoland, natural size, side view during active swimming; the flattened jelly disc contracts almost hemispherically, expelling water and setting the wreath of long tentacles into a graceful wave motion; the stomach hangs centrally with 50-70 radial canals radiating from it.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: From the Indian Ocean, natural size, side view; the high-arched, crystal-bell-like jelly disc has radiating ribs and numerous long tentacles at its margin; the stomach stalk splits into 16 long, curled, wave-moving mouth lobes, and each forked radial canal bears a folded gonad.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Caught near the Azores, natural size, viewed half from below and half from the side; a thick gelatinous stomach stalk splits near its base into 32 long, thin, curling mouth lobes above a wreath of 32 gonads; distinguished from the related Orchistoma Steenstrupi of the Antilles by its slenderer stalk and longer mouth lobes and tentacles.

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Staatsquallen (Siphonophorae); Ordnung der Prachtquallen (Physonectae); Familie der Discolabiden.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Complete siphonophore colony caught in the Indian Ocean in December 1881, drawn from life at Billiton, shown at double natural size; the swimming body bears a gas-filled float and four rows of swimming bells, while the nutritive body carries tentacle-bearing feeding polyps and gonad clusters producing thousands of sexual persons.

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Allman
figures.note: From a creeping, thread-like rootstock rise four long-stalked feeding polyps and two short-stalked reproductive polyps (gonangia) containing several medusa buds and lacking mouth or tentacles; only one hydranth still shows its mouth and tentacle crown, the others show only the empty cup (hydrotheca).

figures.author: Hincks
figures.note: The two kinds of polyps sit in very different cups: slender, egg-shaped hydrothecae with lid-like toothed margins for the feeding polyps, versus thick, cone-shaped gonangia with a smooth aperture (holding two, four, or eight planula larvae) for the mouthless reproductive polyps.

figures.author: Hincks
figures.note: Sparsely branched colony bearing three kinds of persons: a large feeding polyp with tentacle crown around an egg-shaped proboscis, an egg-shaped, ring-walled reproductive polyp, and three slender, mobile, snake-like nematophores whose mouthless terminal knob sends out many long nettle threads.

figures.author: Allman
figures.note: Three long-stalked feeding polyps rise from the creeping rootstock, only partly retractable into a hemispherical, thick-walled cup; two short-stalked gonangia beside them hold egg-shaped, mouthless reproductive polyps.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Branch of a much-branched colony bearing several feeding polyps and, further down, two larger egg-shaped reproductive polyps (without mouth or tentacles) that each bud off numerous small medusae, later released in the form shown in fig. 8.

figures.author: Haeckel

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Schleierquallen (Craspedotae); Ordnung der Blumenquallen (Anthomedusae).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: View from above of the nearly spherical medusa, magnified 4x; shows the cross of four radial canals, four red folded gonads beneath, the forked, strongly branched oral-arm tips, and numerous ruffled tentacles in eight bundles at the margin, each bundle topped by an eye.

figures.author: L. Agassiz

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel

taxonomy: Stamm der Gliedertiere (Articulata); Hauptklasse der Krustentiere (Crustacea); Klasse der Schildtiere (Aspidonia).

figures.note: Adult male, dorsal view, one-third natural size; body in three parts: a crescent-shaped cephalothorax with four eyes (a small simple pair in front, a large compound pair behind), a six-sided abdomen with six pairs of lateral spines, and a simple strong tail spine.

Larva stage; lacks a tail spine but instead bears a trilobite-like tail-shield (pygidium), earning the name 'trilobite larva' and offered as evidence that horseshoe crabs descend from trilobites.

figures.author: Eichwald

Bilateral larva, highly magnified, viewed from the ventral side; a continuous ciliary swimming band drawn into several symmetrical lobes borders the body's ventral margin, with a pair of round calcareous wheels at the posterior end and the gut visible through the transparent body.

The same bilateral larva, further developed, its ciliary band longer and more strongly curved; a pair of bean-shaped coelomic pouches has pinched off from the stomach, and a five-pointed tube has asymmetrically pinched off from the front of the left pouch.

Barrel-shaped larva developed from the bilateral slipper-shaped larva through a peculiar transformation; the continuous ciliary band is replaced by 5 separate ciliary girdles, and the mouth above is surrounded by 5 tentacles.

Five longitudinal muscles show through the transparent body wall around the spirally coiled gut; calcareous wheels are visible behind, and branched calcareous rods ring the base of the five-rayed tentacle crown in front.

Cross-section through the front of the barrel-shaped larva (fig. 6); the five-sided oral shield at center is surrounded by the nerve ring, whose five thickened cells send out the five main nerve trunks, with the ring-shaped cross-sections of the five hollow primary tentacles between them.

figures.author: Lamarck
figures.note: Same species as fig. 9, outer-side view showing six broad leaf-shaped ribs curving from the hexagonal aperture's rim to its base.

figures.author: Darwin
figures.note: View from the upper open side; six fan-shaped ribs radiate from the corners of the hexagonal aperture, broader than in Coronula diadema.

figures.author: Darwin
figures.note: Cone-shaped shell with six broad-ribbed, fan-shaped calcareous plates radiating from the aperture rim, the aperture closed by four triangular operculum plates.

figures.author: Darwin
figures.note: Elliptical shell built of many small scales, its upper aperture closed by four triangular plates and surrounded by eight larger fan-shaped plates.

figures.author: Sowerby
figures.note: Shell made of eight fan-shaped, delicately ribbed and crenellated plates, with the aperture closed by four triangular plates.

figures.author: Thompson
figures.note: Natural-size ventral view of a shore crab (Carcinus maenas) whose flesh is riddled with the root-like branching absorptive tubes of this parasitic barnacle, whose white body is attached beneath the crab's short tail.

taxonomy: Stamm der Gliedertiere (Articulata); Hauptklasse der Lufttrohrtiere (Tracheata); Klasse der Kerbtiere (Insecta); Ordnung der Schmetterlinge (Lepidoptera); Unterordnung der Kleinschmetterlinge (Microlepidoptera); Familien der Federmotten (Pterophorida, Fig. 1-3) und der eigentlichen Motten (Tineida, Fig. 4-6).

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Wingspan 15mm, shown 8x magnified; brown moth with yellow or grey zigzag cross-bands and 24 delicate plumes, both fore- and hindwings split into six feathered rays each.

figures.author: Hübner
figures.note: Wingspan 30mm, shown 6x magnified; entirely snow-white moth, forewings split into two lobes and hindwings into three, with silvery-white fringes on its five feather pairs; individual scales shown highly magnified (figs. 2a, 2b).

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Wingspan 24mm, shown 5x magnified; yellowish-reddish moth with two-lobed forewings marked by white bands and a brown crossband, and three-lobed, heavily fringed hindwings with a brown spot near the tip.

figures.author: Treitschke
figures.note: Wingspan 8mm, shown 15x magnified; brownish moth with narrow white markings on the forewings and very narrow, long-fringed, brownish-grey hindwings.

figures.author: Zeller
figures.note: Wingspan 20mm, shown 7x magnified; brownish moth with harp-shaped, hook-tipped forewings and elongated reddish silver-grey hindwings; individual scales shown highly magnified (figs. 5a, 5b).

figures.author: Schrank
figures.note: Wingspan 19mm, shown 7x magnified; yellowish moth whose forewings are divided by two pale-yellow triangular spots into an ochre inner field with silvery-green streaks and a yellow-brown outer field with dark stripes.

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Staatsquallen (Siphonophorae); Ordnung der Physoquallen (Physonectae).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The whole colony (cormus) shown free-swimming at natural size, caught in 1881 in the Indian Ocean off Ceylon (Matura); a translucent, mostly pale-bluish colonial siphonophore of thousands of jellyfish-like zooids, closely related to Forskalia.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The gas-filled float (pneumatophore) seen from above, its summit pierced by a central air-pore ringed by an eight-rayed red pigment star thought to serve as a light-sensitive eye.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A cormidium (person-group) under its protective bract-scales, showing the four-part feeding siphon (stalk, base-stomach, stomach with eight red liver stripes, and mouth-bearing trunk) and a long tentacle with short red side-filaments.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A cormidium with the feeding siphon removed, showing the female and male gonophore clusters, the red-mouthed excretory tube (cyston), and the slender spindle-shaped palpon.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A cormidium with its bracts removed, showing the female and male gonophore clusters attached side by side on the stem alongside the large siphon, the cyston, and the palpon.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A strongly magnified lateral filament (tentillum) of the tentacle bearing a red, spirally coiled stinging-cell battery of thousands of venomous nematocysts.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A female zooid (gonophore), a bell-shaped medusa bearing a spherical egg with a large germinal vesicle, seen from the side, with four red nettle-knobs at the ends of its radial canals.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The same female zooid as fig. 7, seen from below.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A male zooid (androphore), a reduced medusa whose large club-shaped stomach sac produces sperm.

taxonomy: Stamm der Sterntiere (Echinodermata); Hauptklasse der Pentorchonia; Klasse der Igelsterne oder Seeigel (Echinidea); Unterklasse der modernen Seeigel (Autechinida); Ordnung der Turbanigel oder Urseeigel (Cidaronia).

figures.author: Lamarck
figures.note: Living animal at natural size, oral view, with the five mouth teeth visible centrally and hundreds of long thin sucker-tipped tube-feet arranged in five paired meridian rows alternating with five paired rows of thick, grooved, toothed spines.

figures.author: Lamarck
figures.note: The oral field of the shell, showing the five mouth teeth, the five narrow perradial ambulacral bands perforated for tube-feet, and the five broader interradial bands bearing large tubercles for the spines.

figures.author: Lamarck
figures.note: The apical (anal) field of the shell, showing the central anus, five small perradial eye-bearing ocellar plates, and five larger interradial genital plates, one enlarged into the pore-filtering madreporite.

figures.author: Agassiz
figures.note: A three-armed pincer organ (pedicellaria).

figures.author: Agassiz
figures.note: A longitudinal section through a pedicellaria (pincer organ).

figures.author: Agassiz
figures.note: A single spine, fluted and decorated with many whorls of small thorns.

figures.author: Agassiz
figures.note: A single spine adorned with several parallel toothed longitudinal ridges.

figures.author: Agassiz
figures.note: The strongly magnified terminal disc of a tube-foot, supported by five latticed calcareous plates.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: A strongly magnified cross-section through a spine, showing concentric lamellae and radial ribs.

figures.author: Desor
figures.note: A three-armed pincer organ (pedicellaria).

figures.author: Desor
figures.note: 'Aristotle's lantern', the internal jaw apparatus bearing the five teeth, made of five large and several small calcareous pieces, already known to Aristotle.

taxonomy: Stamm der Urtiere (Protozoa); Hauptklasse der Wurzelfüßer (Rhizopoda); Klasse der Strahlinge (Radiolaria); Legion der Cannopyleen (Phaeodaria).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial tube is knob-shaped and swollen, bearing a wreath of 6-9 curved hollow end-branches armed with barbs and crowned at the tip with a spine-star (Spathilla).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial tube is cushion-shaped and swollen, bearing two alternating wreaths of straight, radially divergent end-branches, each with two opposite rows of pointed teeth and a spine-star at the tip.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial spine is egg-shaped and swollen, bearing 20-30 weakly curved end-branches arranged in five meridian rows and 4-6 concentric whorls, each branch with two opposite rows of barbs and a spine-star at the tip.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial tube bears a wreath of 6-9 straight, crowned end-branches.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial tube is fork-shaped, bearing three smooth, strongly curved branches ending in four spines.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial tube forms a trident with three smooth, curved end-branches.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial spine bears two or three smooth, curved end-branches.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Outer end of each radial spine bears four smooth, strongly recurved barbs.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Single-celled spherical body with central capsule containing a nucleus; skeleton forms a delicate lattice sphere of triangular meshes, each group of six meshes topped by a tent-shaped pyramid with a radial rod ending in a spine-crowned radiation sphere (fig. 10 shows this sphere further magnified).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A skeletal rod that, instead of the radiation sphere of fig. 10, bears a delicate end-head made of four vertical feathered blades.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A skeletal rod with divergent end-branches that bear a spine-star (Spathilla) at the tip.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The two-valved lattice shell bears two horns (one per valve) at the hinged posterior end where the valves join.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The two-valved lattice shell bears four strong curved horns, one at the rear and one at the apex of each valve; the slightly separated valve edges show numerous interlocking pointed teeth, like many bivalve mollusks.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: One of three bristle-like styles arising from the helmet-cap at the apex of each shell valve.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: One of four styles arising from the helmet-cap at the apex of each shell valve.

taxonomy: Stamm der Blumenpflanzen (Phanerogamae oder Anthophyta); Hauptklasse der Bedecktsamigen (Angiospermae); Klasse der Zweikeimblättrigen (Dicotyleae); Legion der Krugpflanzen (Sarraceniaceae); Familie der Kannenpflanzen (Nepenthaceae).

figures.author: Reinwardt
figures.note: Purple-brown pitcher plant of the Malay Archipelago (Java), painted from a specimen found 4 January 1901 at the Tjiburrum waterfalls; the pitcher is a modified leaf-tip that traps insects on a waxy slippery inner surface and digests them with an acid, pepsin-like fluid; shown reduced by one third.

taxonomy: Stamm der Pilze (Fungi); Hauptklasse der Ständerpilze (Basidiomycetes, Basimycetes); Klasse der Bauchpilze (Gastromycetes); Legion der Stinkmorcheln (Phalloideae).

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Common stinkhorn of Europe, natural size; egg-shaped volva cut through the middle to show its chambered wall and the hollow cylindrical stalk, which bears an olive-green cap with a coarse net-patterned surface.

figures.author: Labillardière
figures.note: Polyp-fungus of Java, natural size; from a volva split into eight lobes rises a hollow red polyp-like fruiting body whose mouth is ringed by eight pairs of tentacle-like lobes.

figures.author: Tournefort
figures.note: Red lattice fungus of Southern Europe, reduced size; hemispherical volva with rooting mycelial strands below and eight triangular lobes above; the red fruiting body forms an egg-shaped lattice cage with wide meshes separated by thick, cross-folded bars.

figures.author: E. Fischer
figures.note: Curly lattice fungus of South America, natural size; globular volva splits into four triangular lobes enclosing an egg-shaped spore receptacle whose lattice bars are strongly wrinkled at the outer edge.

figures.author: E. Fischer
figures.note: Small lattice fungus of Australia, natural size; hemispherical volva splits into ten egg-shaped lobes at the mouth; the emerging spore receptacle forms a vault of six cross-wrinkled columns joined above in a ring.

figures.author: Montagne
figures.note: Polyp-cup fungus of the West Indies, natural size; cup-shaped fruiting body whose rim bears numerous inward-curved, polyp-arm-like appendages, its base forming the globular volva.

figures.author: Klotzsch
figures.note: Round-headed stalked fungus of America, reduced size; a reddish stalk sits in a six-lobed globular volva and bears a lattice-shaped fruiting body whose wrinkled bars carry the spore mass at the base.

figures.author: Burt
figures.note: Star-flower fungus of North America, enlarged; cross-section through the top of a young fruiting body shows a central gelatinous strand from which six ray-shaped mesh plates radiate, dividing the stalk into six spore-filled chambers.

figures.author: Micheli
figures.note: Many-rayed earthstar fungus of Europe, natural size; the rounded fruiting body's tough outer envelope splits into star-shaped strips forming a wreath of rolled-back lobes around the delicate inner envelope.

figures.author: O.F. Müller
figures.note: Shaggy ink cap (shaggy mane) of Europe, reduced size; from a cylindrical volva rises a slender stalk bearing a cylindrical yellowish cap whose outer surface is covered with scaly flakes.

taxonomy: Stamm der Urpflanzen (Protophyta); Hauptklasse der Algetten (Zoosporatae); Klasse der Riesen-Algetten (Siphoneae).

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Cluster-bearing Caulerpa from the Red Sea coral reefs; branch-tips of the giant single cell form grape-like clusters of club-shaped berries, with finely branched fiber roots.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Berry-bearing Caulerpa from the Ceylon coral reefs; branch-tips form clusters of wine-grape-like vesicles, with finely branched fiber roots.

figures.author: Weber van Bosse
figures.note: Feathered Caulerpa from the coral reefs of the Malay Archipelago; branch-tips resemble the feathered fronds of a fern.

figures.author: Lamouroux
figures.note: Cup-bearing Caulerpa from the coast of Samoa; branch-tips resemble a stack of dishes or cups pierced through the middle by a stalk and arranged in tiers.

figures.author: Harvey
figures.note: Clubmoss-like Caulerpa from the coast of Florida; branch-tips resemble the bushy, leaf-covered branches of clubmoss (Lycopodium).

figures.author: Decaisne
figures.note: Shield-bearing Caulerpa from the coral reefs of Celebes; branch-tips form a stalked, circular, often three- or four-parted shield bearing a delicate lattice of ribs.

figures.author: Sonder
figures.note: Feather-shaped alga from the coasts of Australia; branch-tips form a doubly feathered leaf, its feather-branches joined by cross-branches into a loose net, anchored below by root branches.

figures.author: Cramer
figures.note: Small-cup-shaped alga from the coast of Madagascar; club-shaped cell (5x magnified in fig. 9) densely covered with strongly folded, facet-like hairy branch-tips; cross-section (fig. 8) shows four segments of the outer lime ring with radial spore-bearing pieces between them.

figures.author: Lamouroux
figures.note: Mushroom-cap-shaped alga (mermaid's wineglass) from the Mediterranean coasts; branch-tips radiate from the top of a thin stalk and fuse so the whole cell resembles a mushroom cap; new thalli form at the rootlike base of the stalk.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Cone-shaped alga from the coral reefs of the Tonga (Friendly) Islands; branch-tips of the club-shaped cell unite into an egg-shaped cone whose hexagonally faceted rind is mostly stripped away to show fourteen whorls of radial branches around the stem.

taxonomy: Stamm der Tange (Algae); Klasse der Rotalgen (Florideae oder Rhodophyceae).

figures.author: Lyngbye
figures.note: Gelatinous-cartilaginous thallus with many repeatedly forked branches, natural size; this species dried yields the official 'carrageen' (Icelandic moss).

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Flat, ribbon-shaped thallus, natural size, with alternating side-shoots bearing further feather-branched secondary shoots on the edge or surface.

figures.author: Postels
figures.note: Thallus, natural size, resembling a branched leafy shoot with a scaly cylindrical stem and radially furrowed, cup-like leaves.

figures.author: Kützing
figures.note: Extremely richly branched thallus, natural size, with feather-like branches bearing feathered branchlets; shoots flattened and two-edged.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Slightly enlarged piece of a side-branch showing alternately feathered branches, smooth on the front concave edge and half-feathered on the rear convex edge, each opposite a sporangium-bearing shoot carrying four sporangia.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Flat, forked, leaf-shaped thallus, natural size, twisted spirally like a staircase with irregularly jagged and fringed free edges.

figures.author: Harvey
figures.note: Narrow leaf-shaped, irregularly branched thallus, natural size, whose branches sprout further shoots from the leaf edge or midrib, their tips delicately rolled inward.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Irregularly branched thallus, natural size, with shoots forming a very thin, broadly lance-shaped leaf with a strong, regularly feathered midrib.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Gelatinous, extremely curly-branched thallus, natural size, resembling a cauliflower head, with forked and lobed thick-edged shoots.

figures.author: Agardh
figures.note: Strongly enlarged vertical section through a fruit-bladder (cystocarpium) showing the narrow canal through which spores exit.

figures.author: Schmitz
figures.note: Strongly enlarged vertical section through a fruit-bladder (cystocarpium) showing small spore-bearing shoots at its base and the upper spore-exit opening.

taxonomy: Stamm der Gliedertiere (Articulata); Hauptklasse der Lufttrohrtiere (Tracheata); Klasse der Spinnentiere (Arachnida).

figures.author: Michael
figures.note: Nymph of a thorn-crowned moss mite from Europe, magnified 90x, body 0.60mm long.

figures.author: Koch
figures.note: Nymph of a spine-wreathed moss mite from Europe, magnified 60x, body 0.90mm long.

figures.author: Nicolet
figures.note: Nymph of a feathered moss mite from Europe, magnified 80x, body 0.62mm long.

figures.author: Michael
figures.note: Nymph of a leaf-girdled moss mite from Europe, magnified 70x, body 1.0mm long.

figures.author: Olivier
figures.note: Kidney-shaped whip scorpion from the East Indies, shown at natural size.

figures.author: Walckenaer
figures.note: Heart-shaped Arkys spider from America, magnified 2x.

figures.author: Latreille
figures.note: Crab-shaped spiny spider from Brazil, magnified.

figures.author: Koch
figures.note: Triangular spiny spider from Madagascar, magnified about 5x.

figures.author: Koch
figures.note: Double-thorned spiny spider from the East Indies, magnified.

figures.author: Koch
figures.note: Arch-thorned spiny spider from Java, magnified 2x.

figures.author: Hahn
figures.note: Six-spined spiny spider from Brazil, magnified 4x.

figures.author: Koch
figures.note: Thick-thorned spiny spider from South America, magnified 2x.

figures.author: Hahn
figures.note: Twin-forked spiny spider from Brazil, magnified 4x.

figures.author: Hahn
figures.note: Mottled lynx spider from Germany, magnified 3x.

figures.author: Linnaeus
figures.note: Garden cross spider from Germany, magnified 3x.

taxonomy: Stamm der Wirbeltiere (Vertebrata); Hauptklasse der Kiefermäuler (Gnathostoma); Klasse der Säugetiere (Mammalia); Unterklasse der Plazentatiere (Placentalia); Ordnung der Fledertiere (Chiroptera).

figures.author: Geoffroy
figures.note: Long-eared bat; ears very large, nearly as long as the body, thin-membraned, with the tragus one-third the ear's length; figure shown slightly reduced in size.

figures.author: Geoffroy
figures.note: Head of the same species, slightly enlarged, front view during excitement, ears folded sideways and toward the tip, tragus lancet-shaped and nearly half as long as the ear.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: The gigantic ears are longer and broader than the head, thin-membraned; the inner ear-flap is rounded at top with projecting teeth at the lower edge; two small transverse leaflets rise above the nostrils.

figures.author: Geoffroy
figures.note: The large ears are fused along the inner margin in their lower half, as long as the head; the tragus is two-thirds as long as the ear; the nose-leaf consists of a lower horseshoe-shaped piece and heart-shaped middle and upper pieces.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: The egg-shaped free ears are about as large as the head, with a small tragus bearing a pointed, toothed process; the nose-leaf consists of a lower horseshoe-shaped and an upper pointed piece.

figures.author: Tomes
figures.note: The egg-shaped ears are very broad and larger than the head; the nose-leaf consists of a lower three-lobed piece and an upper narrow triangular, ridged piece resembling a lance-point, longer than the head.

figures.author: Tomes
figures.note: Head of the same species seen half from behind and half from the left side, showing the same ear and nose-leaf structure.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: The broad ears are obliquely egg-shaped, about as long and broad as the head; the tragus is small and nearly half-moon shaped; nostrils open at the tip of the snout, and the upper lip bears a broad mustache.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: The large, nearly quadrangular ears have two notches on the upper outer margin and are two-thirds as long as the head; the chin bears a large quadrangular, lobed and warty skin plate.

figures.author: Thomas
figures.note: This 'three-cup nose', closely related to the European horseshoe bat, has a lower horseshoe-shaped nose-leaf divided into several paired lobes and a stalked, fan-shaped upper leaf bearing three parallel, thin-stalked cups.

figures.author: Pallas
figures.note: The narrow ears are egg-triangular with a tragus half as long as the ear; the lower horseshoe-shaped nose-leaf is enclosed by a toothed half-moon, the upper egg-shaped leaf pointed.

figures.author: Tomes
figures.note: The ears are roundish, as long as broad, with a small ear-flap shaped like an arrowhead.

figures.author: Schreber
figures.note: The triangular ears are cross-ribbed and feathered on the inner margin; the lower nose-leaf shows a horseshoe with three parallel arch pairs, the small upper leaf forms an equilateral triangle with two notches.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: The outer ear and the small tragus are each divided into two lobes; the lower nose-leaf forms a quadrangular shield flanked by the nostrils and surrounded by six knots, the upper leaf forming three superimposed horseshoe arches.

figures.author: Geoffroy
figures.note: The egg-shaped ears are as large as the head, with a narrow, pointed tragus one-third the ear's length; the nose-appendage is narrow, with a lower horseshoe leaf and an upper lance-point leaf.

taxonomy: Stamm der Wirbeltiere (Vertebrata); Hauptklasse der Kiefermäuler (Gnathostoma); Klasse der Lurche (Amphibia); Unterklasse der Nacktlurche (Lissamphibia); Legion der Frösche (Batrachia oder Anura, Ecaudata); Ordnungen der Erdfrösche (Ranacea) und der Laubfrösche (Hylacea).

figures.author: Weinland
figures.note: Pouched frog of Venezuela; the female has a paired back-pouch where eggs develop into tadpoles, entered through a triangular slit at the rear of the back.

figures.author: Boulenger
figures.note: Tree frog of North Africa and Southern Europe, similar to the common green tree frog; the male inflates its throat skin like a bladder when calling.

figures.author: Boulenger
figures.note: Tree frog of Ecuador with thick fingers bearing very broad adhesive discs and granular, wart-covered skin like a toad.

figures.author: Boulenger
figures.note: Climbing frog of Ecuador with extremely thin, long, zebra-striped limbs suited to agile climbing.

figures.author: Wallace
figures.note: Flying frog of Borneo with greatly broadened webbing between the toes, used as a parachute during long leaps between trees, similar to flying dragons and flying squirrels.

figures.author: Schneider
figures.note: Frog of Surinam whose female carries 12-20 tadpoles on her back, attached by mouth-suckers to two ridges symmetrical about the midline, tails pointing outward.

figures.author: Duméril
figures.note: Banded frog of Java with two white longitudinal bands on a dark reddish-brown back, shown catching an insect with its forked tongue.

figures.author: Boulenger
figures.note: Horned frog of the Solomon Islands with a pair of pointed horns on the triangular head (elongated eyelid extensions); coloring highly variable, often camouflaged.

figures.author: Peters
figures.note: Thick-headed frog of East Africa with a very short, thick head and weak legs unable to jump; digs into the ground with a shovel-like hind-foot callus and feeds on termites, mole-like.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Leopard frog of North America, showing a large, superficial white eardrum just behind the eye.

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Korallen (Anthozoa); Legion der Sternkorallen (Zoantharia); Ordnung der Sechsstrahligen Sternkorallen (Hexacoralla).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: New species from Singapore in the 'Crateriformis' species-group, closest to T. undata; distinguished by a second, smaller funnel-shaped colony rising from the middle of the first, with strongly wave-folded thin walls.

figures.author: Henry Bernard
figures.note: Species in the 'Foliata' group with notably thicker, more robust wave-folded funnel walls and larger, denser egg-shaped polyps than the previous species.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Colony built of upright, partly branched, wave-folded leaves bearing small polyps in parallel transverse rows separated by horizontal ridges.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Close relative of L. frondifera with stronger, more irregularly twisted leaves and strong ascending ribs crossing the horizontal ridges.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: New species from Sumatra, intermediate between H. exesa and H. lobata; distinguished by grape-cluster-like branching and egg-shaped polyps densely packed on club-shaped end-branches.

figures.author: Blainville
figures.note: Colony (a quarter shown) shaped like a round lettuce-head with thin, twisted, torn leaves and very irregular, deeply funnel-shaped polyp calices.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Colony resembling a folded ruff, formed as a simple funnel-shaped polyp elongates and its opposing walls fold into regular pleats with feathered septa.

figures.author: Oken
figures.note: Group of two single polyps whose funnel-shaped upper surface is crossed by radial septa, twelve of them (six primary, six secondary) stronger and strongly serrated.

figures.author: Dana
figures.note: Colony divided into sub-colonies by deep incisions, with densely packed, irregularly polygonal funnel-shaped polyps.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Similarly built to A. magnifica but spread flat on the ground, with fairly regular polygonal polyp calices.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Colony of few (originally six) very elongated, narrow feathered-leaf-shaped polyps whose outer ends are beginning to divide again.

figures.author: Milne-Edwards
figures.note: Nearly spherical colony (a third shown) of mostly free polyps joined only at the root, with finely ribbed, cylindrical, somewhat compressed calices.

taxonomy: Stamm der Sterntiere (Echinoderma); Hauptklasse der Fünfstrahler (Pentorchonia); Klasse der Schlangensterne (Ophiodea); Ordnung der Euryalen (Cladophiura).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: New species from the Indian Ocean (Sumatra), closest to A. muricatum and A. Lincku; distinguished by blunt spines covering the back and by the ten radial ribs of the disc fusing pairwise into a heart-shaped mass; fig. 1 whole animal from below, fig. 2 disc from above.

figures.author: Lyman
figures.note: Middle five-sided part of the scale-bearing circular disc, with the basal starting piece of two arms.

figures.author: Lyman
figures.note: Lower part of the disc seen in profile, showing the scale-wreaths protecting the basal parts of the five arms.

figures.author: Lyman
figures.note: Skeleton of a single arm-joint near the tip, with a pair of forked side-plates bearing thin knobbed lime-spines spread radially like umbrella ribs.

figures.author: Lyman
figures.note: Upper view of the five-sided central disc and adjoining marginal area with the basal joints of two arms.

figures.author: Lyman
figures.note: View of the mouth from below, showing five two-pointed teeth on jaw-plates, paired finger-shaped oral tentacles, and fifteen surrounding limestone shield plates.

taxonomy: Stamm der Urtiere (Protozoa); Hauptklasse der Wurzelfüßer (Rhizopoda); Klasse der Strahlinge (Radiolaria); Legion der Korbstrahlinge oder Monopyleen (Nassellaria); Ordnung der Ringelstrahlinge (Stephoidea).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Egg-shaped central capsule (red) holds the podoconus below and a sausage-shaped nucleus above, with oil globules at the sides; a single vertical silica ring forms the main skeleton.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Skeleton of two perpendicular silica rings, a vertical ring (as in fig. 1) plus a horizontal ring below, with strongly branched pseudopodia radiating outward.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Numerous symbiotic yellow algal cells (Xanthellae) scattered in the calymma; a vertical elliptical silica ring enclosing the calymma bears many antler-branched spines, giving a crown-like skeleton.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Skeleton of three silica rings set in three mutually perpendicular planes; the horizontal ring sits lower than the middle of the two vertical rings, so the four upper gates are larger than the four lower ones.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Spherical red central capsule enclosed by a concentric spherical gelatinous calymma bearing three circular silica rings in three perpendicular planes, leaving eight equal, equilateral triangular gates open.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Two equal-sized horizontal rings curve toward each other and fuse at both poles of the horizontal axis, leaving eight large gates open between them and the smaller vertical ring.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A third (equatorial) horizontal ring sits between the upper (mitral) and lower (basal) rings; all three are bisected by the vertical sagittal ring.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Two horizontal rings joined by six vertical pillars (halves of three meridian rings); a summit spine on top and three divergent spiny feet below.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Diadem-like silica shell with a very strong, thorny apical spine above and four short vertical feet at the base.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Skeleton of two horizontal and four vertical rings intersecting in the vertical median plane; numerous yellow Xanthella cells and fine pseudopodia radiate from the red central capsule between the leaf-widened spines.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Drum-shaped silica shell whose two drumheads are replaced by a vaulted lattice plate; the two horizontal rings are joined by 10-12 parallel vertical rods.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Crown-like skeleton of two parallel horizontal rings joined by eight rods; since the lower (basal) ring is twice the diameter of the upper (mitral) ring, the rods slope obliquely, each ending in a toothed spine at both ends.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Two equal-sized, square horizontal silica rings joined at their four corners by four parallel vertical rods, forming a cube-shaped frame with six square gates.

taxonomy: Stamm der Vorkeimpflanzen (Diaphyta oder Archegoniata); Hauptklasse der Mooßpflanzen (Bryophyta); Klasse der Laubmoose (Muscinae).

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: The gracefully curved 'fox-tail moss', one of the tallest tree-like moss species of its region, with sturdy dark-green, richly leaved branches.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Delicate climbing 'vine moss' with very fine trailing shoots that entwine the branches of Thamnium alopecurum.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Tall 'grenadier moss' whose helmet-like fruits are covered by a bell-shaped, felted hood (calyptra) that is later shed.

figures.author: Ehrhart
figures.note: Peat moss with slender, pale, toothed leaves forming two regular whorls at the top, topped by a wreath of small knob-shaped, long-stalked fruits.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Delicate 'umbrella moss' whose small fruits bear an unusually large shield-shaped yellow appendage resembling an open umbrella.

figures.author: Hedwig
figures.note: 'Star moss' with a lush star-shaped leaf rosette from whose center slender red stalks bear a cluster of nodding fruits with finely toothed mouths.

figures.author: Schreber
figures.note: 'Rose moss' with three long, likewise nodding fruit stalks rising from the center of a star-shaped leaf rosette.

figures.author: Schleicher
figures.note: Small urns of this dwarf bladder-moss.

figures.author: Notaris
figures.note: Cone-shaped fruits capped with a pointed hood.

figures.author: Schwaegrichen
figures.note: Spherical urn-shaped fruits.

figures.author: Limpricht
figures.note: Three reddish little fruiting heads of this peat moss lying at the forest floor.

figures.author: Schimper
figures.note: Scale-leaved 'stone moss' with four stems; of its three red fruits, one is still closed while two have split open into four valves.

figures.author: Linné
figures.note: Doubly feathered 'fern moss' forming three broad triangular tufts closely resembling small fern fronds.

figures.author: Schimper
figures.note: A tuft of this 'umbrella moss' in the foreground.

figures.author: Greville
figures.note: Small 'double-tooth moss' shown on the left.

figures.author: Hedwig
figures.note: Small 'double-tooth moss' shown alongside D. Hornschuchii.

taxonomy: Stamm der Pilze (Fungi oder Mycetes); Klasse der Schlauchpilze (Ascomycetes oder Ascosporomycetes); Legion der Fruchtkapselpilze (Carpascodii).

figures.author: De Candolle
figures.note: Powdery mildew of the barberry, living on leaves of Berberis vulgaris; the round, nearly spherical fruiting body is ringed at the base by delicate, repeatedly forked, antler-like hairs.

figures.author: De Candolle
figures.note: Powdery mildew of the alder, on leaves of Alnus glutinosa; the round, slightly flattened fruiting body is ringed at the equator by 10-16 hairs ending in short forked, antler-like branches.

figures.author: De Candolle
figures.note: Powdery mildew of the goat willow, on leaves of Salix caprea; the round, flattened-spherical fruiting body is ringed by numerous hairs with blunt, inward-curved ends.

figures.author: De Candolle
figures.note: Powdery mildew of the sycamore maple, on leaves of Acer pseudoplatanus; shown cut vertically with the front half removed, revealing spindle-shaped spore-sacs (each with eight spores) interspersed with sterile paraphyses, topped by a wreath of forked hairs.

figures.author: Tulasne
figures.note: Fungus on dead branches of the beech (Fagus silvatica); the spherical fruiting body, shown cut vertically and strongly magnified, has a thick shell opened by a pore at the top, filled with cylindrical eight-spored sacs and paraphyses, ringed at the base by a velvety conidial swelling.

figures.author: Tulasne
figures.note: Fungal parasite on the bolete Boletus tomentosus; loose threads bear two kinds of conidia, larger golden-yellow spiny macroconidia and smaller snow-white smooth microconidia.

figures.author: Tulasne
figures.note: Fungal parasite on gilled mushrooms (Agaricus species); the mycelium produces spherical or pear-shaped spore-bearing fruit bodies, branched threads bearing spiny macroconidia, and long jointed threads whose segments detach to form small microconidia.

figures.author: Tulasne
figures.note: Sooty fungus on dead oak bark (Quercus); a group of spindle-shaped, long-stalked conidial fruits, each enclosing a chain of 4-8 conidia.

figures.author: Tulasne
figures.note: Variable sooty fungus of many herbs; the pictured form developed on winter-frost-killed fruits of Cucurbita, its conidia enclosed in stalked conidial fruits.

taxonomy: Stamm der Blütenpflanzen (Phanerogamae oder Anthophyta); Hauptklasse der Bedecktsamigen (Angiospermae); Klasse der Einsamenlappigen (Monocotylae); Legion der Säulengriffler (Gynandrae); Familie der Venusblumen oder Kuckucksblüten (Orchideae).

figures.author: Johannes Müller
figures.note: Free-swimming trematode larva of the genus Distoma with two round suckers, a forked yellow gut, coiled excretory canals, and an undivided mobile tail with a thin fin-like skin seam.

figures.author: La Valette
figures.note: Differs from Cercaria dichotoma by a spiny neck-collar behind the anterior sucker and a forked mobile tail.

figures.author: Ercolani
figures.note: Distinguished by a doubled, strongly developed mobile tail; when spirally coiled forward it resembles a ram's or ox's head (hence originally described as Bucephalus polymorphus); the mature form, Gasterostomum fimbriatum, lives in the gut of freshwater fish infected by eating mussels harboring the larvae.

figures.author: Rudolphi
figures.note: Mature fluke living in the frog's urinary bladder, attached by a posterior sucker-disc bearing three pairs of large round suckers; the gut forms a rare ring shape.

figures.author: Rudolphi
figures.note: Free-swimming larva of the same species, swimming by five ciliated girdles before penetrating the gill cavity of tadpoles and migrating to the bladder during metamorphosis.

figures.author: Nordmann
figures.note: Fluke living on the gills of carp and other freshwater fish, bearing a large posterior sucker-disc with 16 hooks.

figures.author: Nordmann
figures.note: The 'double animal', living on the gills of freshwater fish, forms when two individuals of the genus Diporpa fuse, the dorsal papilla of one joining the ventral sucker of the other.

figures.author: Cuvier
figures.note: Disc-shaped, flattened fluke parasitic on fish, attached by two lateral mouth-suckers and a large wheel-shaped ventral sucker; the gut forms a triangular, much-branched ring.

figures.author: Diesing
figures.note: Fluke with a small anterior mouth-sucker and a large wheel-shaped ventral sucker behind a simple forked gut.

figures.author: Rudolphi
figures.note: Unsegmented carnation-worm living in the gut of carp, representing the simple tapeworms (Monocestoda); its internal organs belong to a complex reproductive apparatus.

figures.author: Cuvier
figures.note: Young chain tapeworm living in fish; the head bears four long, mobile proboscises, the trunk many short, broad proglottids.

figures.author: Van Beneden
figures.note: Cross-shaped head of a chain tapeworm living in rays, bearing four large, curled, very mobile adhesive lobes.

figures.author: Rudolphi
figures.note: A single mature proglottid of the human tapeworm, whose chain reaches 2-3m and consists of 800-900 segments, showing the branched, translucent uterus.

figures.author: Rudolphi
figures.note: The scolex (head), viewed from the apex; the central rostellum is ringed by 25-28 hooks, with four large round suckers arranged crosswise at the margin.

taxonomy: Stamm der Gliedertiere (Articulata); Hauptklasse der Krustentiere (Crustacea); Klasse der Krebstiere (Caridonia); Legion der Panzerkrebse (Thoracostraca).

figures.author: Milne Edwards
figures.note: Gastrula stage, the two-layered germ common to all multicellular animals (Metazoa) and absent in single-celled Protozoa; the endoderm encloses the archenteron opening through the blastopore, the ectoderm forms the outer skin.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Nauplius larva common to all true crustaceans; the pear-shaped body bears three jointed leg pairs that become the anterior antenna, posterior antenna, and mandible.

figures.author: Spence Bate
figures.note: Larva of Sergestes tenuis, bearing a row of curved spines along its back.

figures.author: Spence Bate
figures.note: Larva of Sergestes elaphocaris, distinguished by an almost square carapace armed with branched spines.

figures.author: Milne Edwards
figures.note: Larva of the common spiny lobster Palinurus vulgaris, appearing as a thin, round, glass-clear disc with only a short abdominal stub, bearing no resemblance to the adult; formerly described as a separate genus, Phyllosoma.

figures.author: Milne Edwards
figures.note: Zoea larva of the common crab Carcinus maenas, with a pair of very large eyes and usually a large frontal spine and curved dorsal spine.

figures.author: Brooks
figures.note: Larva of the mantis shrimp Gonodactylus chiragra; the carapace ends in a strong spine front and back, with a straight keel along the abdomen's back.

figures.author: Brooks
figures.note: Early larva of Squilla gracilis; larvae of Squilla differ so greatly across metamorphic stages that they were formerly classed as separate genera (Erichthoidina, Alima, Erichthus).

figures.author: Brooks
figures.note: Later larval stage of Squilla gracilis, showing the abdomen still small relative to its size in the adult.

figures.author: Claus
figures.note: Larva of Squilla mantis, distinguished by an elongated second maxilliped forming a knife-shaped grasping claw; the abdomen's rear segments each bear a gill with 4-5 half-feathered branches.

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Staatsquallen (Siphonophorae); Ordnung der Kelchquallen (Calyconectae).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The whole colony from the Canary Islands, natural size; two large, nearly equal egg-shaped swimming bells with edgeless margins sit at the tip of a long mobile stem bearing very numerous cormidia at wide, regular intervals.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A single cormidium (described separately as Eudoxella galea), weakly enlarged; the sterile medusa person has an irregular kidney-shaped bell with four unequal radial canals and a barrel-shaped gut with eight yellow liver stripes, while the fertile person is a four-canaled medusa bell bearing the sperm gland.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The whole colony from the Canary Islands, natural size; the upper swimming bell is a small five-sided prism with a horizontal axis, the lower is a larger four-sided obelisk with a vertical axis, joined by the stem bearing regularly spaced cormidia.

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: The lower (basal) swimming bell viewed from below, with four ear-shaped triangular lobes, a ring canal giving off four radial canals, and a funnel canal hiding the contracted nutritive body.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: A single cormidium (described separately as Sphenoides obeliscus), weakly enlarged; the larger sterile medusa bears twelve pyramidal projections and a barrel-shaped gut with a long tentacle whose lateral filaments carry venomous stinging batteries, alongside a four-lobed fertile male medusa.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: An isolated female reproductive individual, its four-sided pyramidal bell differing in shape from the male shown in fig. 7, with the ovary hanging in the base of the bell cavity.

taxonomy: Stamm der Nesseltiere (Cnidaria); Klasse der Lappenquallen (Acraspedae); Ordnung der Würfelquallen (Cubomedusae).

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from the southern Atlantic (near Saint Helena), natural size; four hand-shaped pedalia, each split into 21 jelly fingers bearing long ringed tentacles; folded gonads and a pear-shaped stomach visible through the transparent wall.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from the Indian Ocean, natural size; cube-shaped disc with four asymmetrically twisted hands, each split into four unequal fingers bearing tentacles.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from West Africa (Cape Verde Islands), double natural size; bell shaped as a truncated four-sided pyramid with eight pairs of longitudinal ridges; four tentacles each bear a nematocyst knob at the tip.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Mouth and stomach of the same species, magnified six times; the flat stomach's mouth is surrounded by four folded, frilled leaf-shaped lobes, with phacellae (gastric filament tufts) visible above.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from West Africa (Sierra Leone), natural size, viewed from below; cross-shaped mouth with four frilled lips surrounded by a velarium with branched canals; deep furrows and egg-shaped pedalia at the four corners.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Same specimen viewed from above; regular cross-shaped stomach lumen with interradial phacellae, thick double pillars at the bell edges, and pedalia with tentacles at their lower ends.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from the Indian Ocean, natural size; egg-shaped bell with four large leaf-shaped pedalia (two shown), each bearing a tentacle; leaf-shaped gonad pairs visible through the transparent wall.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Cube jelly from the West Indies, natural size; tall four-sided prismatic bell twice as high as broad, with band-shaped frilled gonads on the inner edge-pillars, a spherical stomach above and four large leaf-shaped mouth lobes below.

taxonomy: Stamm der Wirbeltiere (Vertebrata); Hauptklasse der Kiefermäuler (Gnathostoma); Klasse der Schleicher (Reptilia); Unterklasse der Schuppenlurche (Lepidosauria); Ordnung der Eidechsen (Lacertilia).

figures.author: Buchholz
figures.note: Horn chameleon from Cameroon; grips branches with prehensile feet and catches insects with a long worm-shaped tongue shot forward suddenly; distinguished by a pair of horn-like protrusions.

figures.author: Dumeril
figures.note: Comb lizard from Java, bearing a long toothed dorsal crest and a wide throat pouch.

figures.author: Linnaeus
figures.note: Flying dragon lizard from Java that glides between trees using a broad lateral skin fold spread by movable ribs, acting as a parachute.

figures.author: Wiegmann
figures.note: Horned lizard from Mexico, covered in pointed horny spines instead of ordinary scales, with an especially large spine crown at the back of the head.

figures.author: Kuhl
figures.note: Fold gecko from Java, distinguished by broad lateral skin folds between fore- and hind-limbs, jaggedly notched along the tail, an early stage of a flight membrane.

figures.author: Daudin
figures.note: Basilisk lizard from Guyana with a tall, spine-supported dorsal crest resembling a fish's dorsal fin.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: Frilled lizard from Australia; the neck bears a large, toothed skin fold resembling a ring collar, spread as a deterrent by moving the elongated hyoid horns supporting it.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: Thorny devil from Australia, entirely covered in thick, cone-shaped spines developed from ordinary skin scales.

taxonomy: Stamm der Sterntiere (Echinodermata); Hauptklasse der Pentorchonia; Klasse der Knospensterne (Blastoidea).

figures.author: Etheridge

figures.author: Troost

figures.author: Roemer

figures.author: Bather

figures.author: Shumard

figures.author: Fr. Schmidt

taxonomy: Stamm der Urtiere (Protozoa); Hauptklasse der Wurzelfüßer (Rhizopoda); Klasse der Kammerlinge (Thalamophora); Ordnung der Siebwandigen (Foraminifera oder Perforata).

figures.note: Whole animal at natural size, seen from below; a new species from the sea off Sumatra, pale reddish with violet gonads, close to the European A. aurita and American A. habanensis but distinguished by four sickle-shaped gonads, short slender arms, and eight deep bays in the umbrella margin housing the sense clubs, the margin fringed with very numerous short tentacles.

figures.author: Lamarck
figures.note: Strongly magnified strobila (budding stack) that produces the moon jelly's alternation of generations: a fertilized egg develops into a simple cup polyp (scyphistoma) whose mouth grows a long stack that segments into numerous circular discs, each with eight sense clubs alternating with eight tentacles, later detaching to swim off as tiny ephyra jellyfish.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Under-view of the circular stomach with 16 radial canals branching from its circumference; the central mouth-cross is surrounded by four ruffled, folded gonads, each with a tuft of gastral filaments along its inner edge.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Side view of the swimming animal at natural size with moving oral lobes and tentacles; the beret-shaped umbrella bears a 16-rayed pigment star, four horseshoe-shaped gonads show through the underside, 24 tentacles sit between eight sense clubs at the margin, and a long oral tube with four large ruffled lips hangs from the underside's center.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Side view of the near-spherical swimming medusa at natural size, with 16 radial rows of large nettle warts between 16 square marginal lobes, alternating with eight sense clubs and eight thread-like tentacles, and four long ruffled oral lobes hanging from the mouth; a horizontal section shows four radial canals alternating with four horseshoe-shaped gonads and gastral filament tufts, plus the nerve ring linking the eight sense clubs; a magnified sense club (rhopalium) shows an egg-shaped, lime-crystal-filled statocyst on top, a star-shaped red pigment eye in the middle, and a smell-pit at the base.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Central section of the umbrella's underside, cut out, showing the mouth-cross with its four lips and arm bases, with delicate curtain-like folded membranes carrying the ruffled gonads between them.

figures.author: Haeckel
figures.note: Shows the underside of the bell after removing the four oral arms and the outer surface of the exumbrella with its distinctive tiling and raised star-ridges; visible are half the central mouth-cross, two of the four crescent-shaped gonads, the eight sense organs separated by 16 five-sided marginal lobes from eight alternating tentacles, and delicately branched gastric canals in the marginal lobes.

taxonomy: Stamm der Wirbeltiere (Vertebrata); Hauptklasse der Kiefermäuler (Gnathostoma); Klasse der Vögel (Aves); Unterklasse der Kielvögel (Carinatae); Ordnung der Luftsegler (Macrochires); Familie der Kolibris (Trochilidae).

figures.author: Blainville
figures.note: Four-horned antelope (Hindi: Bherki); body 85cm, tail 15cm, shoulder height 50cm, brown above and white below; lives in wooded hills of East India; the only living mammal that naturally bears two pairs of horns.

figures.author: Sundevall
figures.note: Wildebeest/gnu; body 2m, tail 80cm, shoulder height 1.4m, dark gray-brown with a whitish-gray mane and tail-tuft; lives in large herds in South Africa, very fast, wild and untameable.

figures.author: Sclater
figures.note: Sitatunga marsh antelope; body 1.2m, shoulder height 90cm, brown with pale stripes and spots; its slender, long legs and elongated splayed hooves are adaptations to living in rivers and swamps of West Africa, as is its coarse shaggy coat.

figures.author: Owen
figures.note: Pronghorn (also called Antilope furcifera, Smith); body 1.25m, tail 20cm, shoulder height 80cm, light reddish-brown above, white below and on the sides; lives on the North American plains in large herds, very fast and shy; its forked horns differ from other antelopes, showing affinities to bighorn sheep and deer.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: Waterbuck (also called Cervicapra ellipsiprymna, Sundevall); body 2m, tail 50cm, shoulder height 1.5m, mostly gray with a yellowish-red tinge and a pale elliptical ring around the tail base, with a strong neck mane; this ox-like antelope lives in the swamps of South Africa and favors staying in water.

figures.author: Harris
figures.note: Sable antelope; body 2.5m, tail 50cm, shoulder height 1.5m, glossy black with white markings in places and a strong neck mane; found in South Africa; both sexes carry very strong, ringed horns curved sharply backward.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: Addax; body 2m, shoulder height 1m, yellowish-white with a brown head, neck and mane, and a white band across the face; found in northeast Africa from Upper Egypt to Lake Chad; both sexes bear long, ringed, slightly lyre-shaped horns.

figures.author: Gray
figures.note: Greater kudu (also called Antilope strepsiceros, Pallas); body 2.5m, tail 0.5m, shoulder height 1.7m, reddish-gray with 7-9 white vertical stripes and a white chevron between the eyes, black neck mane; the strong spirally-twisted horns are yellow-brown and over 1m long; found in wooded central African regions.

figures.author: Sundevall
figures.note: Bushbuck ('harness antelope', also called Antilope maculata, Pallas); body 1.3m, tail 15cm, shoulder height 85cm, chestnut-brown with bold cross-bands, stripes and rows of white spots resembling a horse's harness straps; horns black, 30cm long; found in western central Africa.
